The spark of life in an automobile was shown to be unbelievably tenacious, through the discovery herewith shown. Flood waters in the San Diego River, at San Diego, California, are shown receding after uncovering an automobile that was buried in the river bottom by a flood in 1916. Another unique feature was that the valves did not even have to be ground. In the upper panel of the picture the car is shown being discovered in the mud and the lower half, the resurrected car-running around the streets.

SUMMER ROOF SCHOOL FOR FRAIL CHILDREN A PHIPPS
INSTITUTE-BOARD OF EDUCATION-EXPERIMENT.

A roof school with unique features for the benefit of frailam undemourished children is a scholastic experiment in Philadelphia. The school has been started on the roof of one of the College Settlement Buildings, the experiment being a joint one of the Phipps Institute, the Board of Education and the College Settlement. The Phipps Institute looks after the management of the school, supplies the nurse and the food, the Board of Education furnishes the teacher, the text books, desks and pupils and the College Settlement gives the use of the roof, shelter, playgrounds, bathing and cooking facilities. When reporting the first morning each night and girl was

supplied with a linen bag containing a toothbrush, tooth powder, mouth wash, wash rag, brush and comb and nailbrush. The teachers and the nurse lined the pupils up for the first lesson after furnishing them with their kits, this lesson being on the use of the tooth brush and the way to keep the face, hands and nails clean. Instruction in cleanliness and proper sanitary care of the person will form a large part of the curriculum and daily schedule, rest, exercise, food and study being attended to in their turn.

The school will open at 8 o'clock each morning, this being the bathing hour. At 8.50 breakfast will be served and at 9 o'clock lessons will begin in the open air and continue to 10.50 with five minutes transmission at the end of each half hour. From 10.50 to 11 o'clock is given over to games, following which the children wash up and then rest till noon, when a hot dinner is served in the dining room of the settlement house. From 1 to 6 o'clock is spent in complete relaxation and rest the children lying extended and sleeping if they desire in the comfortable couch chairs provided for the purpose. From 3 o'clock to 4.50 lessons and educational games are conducted and then rest and play occupy the time to the closing hour which is 5.30, a good wash all around closing the school day for the pupils before they are sent home.

A substantial wooden roof over the portion of the school used for class purposes protects the pupils from a treeer rays of the sun and from rain and canvas sised which roll up and down will prevent the beating in of storms or let in the air as may be necessary. The boys and girls are selected from the sickly and aneamy

children attending school within walking distance of the new roof school. Each child is carefully weighed at the beginning of the school attendance and a record kept of the gain each day will show how these school life is helping to build the children up constitutionally.

OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPHS OF THE EXEDITIONARY FORCES IN MEXICO. PASED BY THE CENSOR.

Unclo SSm's boys in Mexico are a hungry crew. They turn up regularly for meals, each with an appetite that is about twice what could be considered the normal consumption of food. This brings up the necessity of having a bakery and a kitchen that can produce large quantities of the nourishing foods.

The bakery at the American base camp in Mexico is quite modern. Pretty near 2000 loaves are turned out daily, and these loaves are not small, each one weighing four pounds after baking. The appliances used are as modern as would be found in the average bakery. The bakers are proficient and the bread they make is good enough to satisfy the hungry trooper. Said trooper often is not so easy to satisfy though he may have a voracious appetite.
The loaves are carefully weighed before baking, each leave has to weigh four pounds and eight ounces. Eight ounces are allowed for evaporation so the broad weighs four pounds when baked.
When thoroughly baked the broad is laid outside the bakery and the supplyergaht of each regiment draws enough bread to serve his band.

THIS BREAD MANER DOES WORK OF 100 MEN TURNING OUT 6000 LOAVES AN HOUR.

Two brothers James and J.H.Garvoy have invented a portable mechanical breed maker that should be a mighty big help in feeding the doughboys in the trenches. Its inventors says that a crew of five men and this broad maker can do the work of a hundred men. It has made 6000 leaves of the staff of life in an hour, a quantity sufficient for 30,000 men. The machine also possesses the advantage, an important one in army work, of mobility. All the apparatus is housed ready for use on an auto-mobile truck ready to start at a moment's notice for anywhere.
